3. Tidal locking happens when a moon's rotation period matches its orbital period, so the same face always points at its planet. Tidal forces raise a bulge that lags or leads the line between the bodies; the resulting torque slows the spin until the bulge stays aligned. Most large moons in the solar system are locked, and many close-in exoplanets are thought to be too, which gives them a permanent day side and night side.
